title: Religious life
hookLine: poverty, chastity and obedience, lived in community

lines: A CARD, READ ALOUD IN A CHAPEL.
cards: A young woman kneels in a chapel before her community: a row of women in the same habit, some old enough to be her grandmother. She holds a card, and her voice shakes a little as she reads from it.
She is promising to own nothing of her own, to love no one as a spouse, and to go where she's sent. In some communities, she then lays the card on the altar and signs it there, in front of everyone.
Afterward, cake in the convent kitchen and family photos. Her brother still doesn't quite get it. Today's word: evangelical counsels.

teach.b: Evangelical here doesn't name a church. It means of the Gospel. The counsels are the Gospel's invitations, as opposed to its commands.

The Catechism draws the line: the commandments are for everyone; the counsels point to ways of removing whatever, even if not wrong, gets in the way of love. It names them: poverty, chastity and obedience. Take poverty.
A rich young man asks Jesus what he still lacks.
In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus answers: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me."
He goes away sad, Matthew says, because he had a great deal. The counsel is the part he couldn't do.
Chastity, for a religious, means celibacy: leaving marriage aside so the heart is free for God and for everyone.
Obedience means putting your will into the hands of the community and its superior, as Jesus put his into the Father's.
The Catechism says it's professing these counsels, in a stable state of life the Church recognizes, that marks consecrated life.
And it's lived together: a shared table, a rule, a chapel, and a superior who sends them.
Not every community words the vows the same way. Benedict's Rule has a monk promise stability, faithfulness to the monastic way of life, and obedience, and Catholics read the same counsels inside it.
Some orders add a vow of their own. The three run underneath.

how: Catholic religious sisters, brothers, monks and nuns profess vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, or a formula that contains them, after a time of formation, and live in community under a rule approved by the Church. Some communities profess an additional vow particular to their mission.

games.q: you're the rich young man. you've kept the commandments, and Jesus tells you to sell what you have, give to the poor, and follow him. what do you do?
o: go away sad, because you have a great deal.
games.why: he goes away sad. the counsel was the part he couldn't do, and the story leaves him there.

practice: Bring to mind a religious sister, brother, monk or nun you've known, seen or read about, and picture them at their ordinary work today.
If you pray, ask God to keep them faithful and glad in their vows, and to send the people their communities need. If you don't, hold them with thanks for one thing they gave away.

wordCard.voice: Evangelical counsels. The Gospel's invitations to poverty, chastity and obedience, which religious sisters and brothers profess as vows and live in community. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the counsels of the Gospel: the Church's name for poverty, chastity and obedience.

carryVoice: Your line: three vows. Each one clears away something that gets in the way of love. Rest well.
